title: Editorial: For the kids | Editorials | rutlandherald.com
text:
Under the umbrella category of “For Future Generations,” certain steps have been taken at the state and federal levels.
Marking two years since the passage of Act 76, Vermont’s historic child care law, Vermont’s Child Care Campaign set priorities for the near future through its “Growing Vermont: A Conversation on the Future of Child Care” and town hall discussion featuring national and local policy experts.
You don’t have to look far to see the challenges facing Vermont families when it comes to child care.
Since the passage of Act 76, Vermont has more than 100 new child care programs have opened, creating more than 1,700 spaces for children and 400 new early childhood educator jobs. In every quarter of 2024, and the first two quarters of 2025, more child care programs have opened than closed.
Vermont families earning up to 575% of the federal poverty level — about $184,862 for a family of four as of October 2024 — are now eligible for tuition assistance. Enrollment in tuition assistance has grown by over 63%, meaning more than 4,700 additional children now benefit from reduced child care costs, according to the coalition making up Vermont’s Child Care Campaign.
In sadder news, Let’s Grow Kids, the advocacy organization launched in 2015 as a 10-year campaign to transform Vermont’s child care system, winds down this year. It will officially cease operations as an organization at the end of this year. Moving forward, Vermont’s Child Care Campaign will be led by child care ecosystem partners: The Vermont Association for the Education of Young Children, Building Bright Futures, First Children’s Finance–Vermont, and the Let’s Grow Kids Action Network.
At the recent gathering of child care advocates, leaders outlined a handful of priorities for the coming year: Protecting current state funding for child care; expanding access and affordability for families; and strengthening the early childhood workforce.
Erin Roche, First Children’s Finance Vermont director, noted: “Expanding access to child care means families have choices and local economies can thrive. Making child care more affordable means families can use their income for things they need and plan for the future. But every new space requires more early childhood educators, access to capital and business know-how to serve their communities for years to come.”
These advocates have been working for Vermont families for years now. They are known for their hard work and commitment to the cause. We have no doubt that their full support will be put into ensuring those commitment and priorities are met for next year, and for the years to come.
At the federal level, we have serious doubts. This administration is not thinking about better tomorrows.
This week, the Make America Healthy Again Commission released its “Make Our Children Healthy Again Strategy.” It is called “a sweeping plan with more than 120 initiatives to reverse the failed policies that fueled America’s childhood chronic disease epidemic.”
According to a news release, “The strategy outlines targeted executive actions to advance gold-standard science, realign incentives, increase public awareness, and strengthen private-sector collaboration.”
Why doubtful? The commission is chaired by U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The commission is tasked with investigating and addressing the root causes of America’s escalating health crisis, with a focus on childhood chronic diseases.
And yet, Kennedy is no fan of vaccines and immunizations — the building blocks of keeping children healthy in the modern era.
“The Trump Administration is mobilizing every part of government to confront the childhood chronic disease epidemic,” Kennedy said in a prepared statement. “This strategy represents the most sweeping reform agenda in modern history — realigning our food and health systems, driving education, and unleashing science to protect America’s children and families. We are ending the corporate capture of public health, restoring transparency, and putting gold-standard science — not special interests — at the center of every decision.”
Why does that feel like children are being used as pawn in a political game? Because they are.
U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke L. Rollins, whose news releases are brimming with propaganda and adoration toward Trump and his policies, continues to do so in response to the MAHA commission report.
“America’s farmers and ranchers are at the heart of the solution — alongside doctors, parents, and communities — to fight chronic disease and protect future generations. Under this Administration, we are not just talking about healthy outcomes; we are delivering them by securing voluntary commitments to remove artificial food dye from major brands, providing technical assistance to States interested in restricting junk food and soda from SNAP, and providing growers with new tools to maintain and improve soil health, including the introduction of a regenerative farming practice pilot program. Together with our partners at HHS and (the Environmental Protection Agency), we are charting a new course, strengthening the health of our families, and ensuring the United States leads the world with the safest, strongest, and most abundant food supply.”
Our question is this: How is politicizing having and raising children actually helping American families?
Taking away critical services and SNAP funding is not proactive. Doing away with vaccines and immunizations is not protecting children. Focusing on privatizing public policy is not a metric toward healthy outcomes.
Toying with our children and families is bad policy. Ask any parent.
